Cindy, alias Cobra, a 18 ans. Elle arriv: Cindy, a.k.a. Cobra, is 18. She arrives at the <l1>Philo-Boxe,</l1> gym at 4:30 p.m., as she does several times a week, ready to jump into the ring. For two years, the shy young boxer has been training with Karim Coppry in a sport that has become her passion. “I love my work, it makes me happy to do it, to share my experience with the community and to be an active part of the social fabric of Côte-des-Neiges,” says Mr. Coppry.
L’intervenant social natif de Côte-des-N: The social worker, who is a Côte-des-Neiges native, created Philo-Boxe, a program that combines sport and discussion and gives young people a place to express themselves. He knows the lives of the neighbourhood’s youth well. “When I was a teenager, I had my own problems; I told myself it would be good to give something back where I grew up,” he explains. Before offering his services in his own neighbourhood, Karim Coppry worked as an urban mediator in Saint-Michel.
À l’époque, le sport n’était pas encore: Back then, sport wasn’t yet on the radar. “I wanted to hold discussions and training sessions for social workers on the subject of biculturalism among young people,” says the social entrepreneur. While rolling out the project with youth organizations, one of them pointed out to him that young people needed stimulating activities. That is how the idea was born of teaching boxing, a sport he took up in his early twenties, and of holding philosophical discussions with his participants.
« Une bonne pratique sportive, à un jeun: “Good sports practice at a young age helps develop discipline,” the boxing coach points out. It can help give young people structure, since regular training requires their presence and attention. However, Mr. Coppry believes that to equip young people, you have to go beyond intervention and help them understand that they have a place in society. “Do young people feel that they have a future? Do they have role models who inspire them, an education about emotions, about the meaning of life?” he asks, believing that a lack of reference points can have a major impact on a teenager’s path.
L’intervenant n’est pas tendre non plus: The social worker is also blunt about the fate reserved for disadvantaged youth. “If you look at the media, they often demonize young people, especially those from another background. They often put violence front and centre, but they don’t give them the chance to speak up.” Making themselves heard is precisely what is difficult, even impossible, for young people. Mr. Coppry says he himself had no opportunity to do so, except when he was among friends or people from his neighbourhood.
Aujourd’hui, le coach espère que ceux qu: Today, the coach hopes that those who came before this generation will become aware and understand that they can change things. “I want people to know that we have the power to act, to put in place actions to support our community, education, the search for meaning and social inclusion,” he says.
Pas besoin d’être sportif pour se mettre: You don’t have to be athletic to start boxing. According to Mr. Coppry, you simply have to want to try. “When we talk about boxing, they think they’re going to hit each other! I explain to them that it’s a boxing workout,” he says of his young recruits. The coach prioritizes young people from the environment where he is working, rather than those who are already interested in sports. That is why the Philo-Boxe program is offered in youth centres. With a mission of making an expensive sport accessible, the non-profit organization offers the program free of charge to participants. Afterwards, the most skilled athletes can train at the Philo-Boxe gym, where they have the chance to improve and, if they wish, to train their peers.
L'équipement est à la disposition des je: Equipment is available to young people at Philo-Boxe. Photo: Pablo Ortiz
C’est le cas de Cobra, qui assiste Karim: That is the case for Cobra, who assists Karim Coppry by teaching young people to box at Chalet Kent, the Côte-des-Neiges youth centre. She enjoys the discussions that emerge from the weekly sessions. “We bring everything we want to talk about in depth, just to discover our point of view and the other person’s,” she says. “We talk about what we feel; we can express ourselves and release all the feelings we have on our hearts,” she explains. As Mr. Coppry points out, the only rule is that the topics raised be tied to their own reality. As a result, the group has ended up talking about its fears, love, history and, why not, ghosts.
Cobra est anxieuse face à l’avenir, qui: Cobra is anxious about the future, which seems uncertain to her. “It’s hard to know if we like what we’re doing, and what impact it will have down the road. If I choose something, what will happen next?” The burden is heavy for many of her peers, she believes. “You feel the pressure to do something big. A lot of people feel the pressure to find work, but it’s hard without experience,” says the young woman, who wants to become a motorcycle mechanic. For now, boxing offers her another path. “With coaching, I feel like I have another option. And I think that’s good,” she reflects.
Cobra à l'entraînement.Photo: Pablo Orti: Cobra in training. Photo: Pablo Ortiz
C’est exactement ce que Philo-Boxe cherc: That is exactly what Philo-Boxe is trying to offer. “In the future, we want to offer other services in the neighbourhood, mentoring, tutoring, coaching, so that young people can develop intervention skills and work experience with Philo-Boxe. We’re really trying to diversify the work experience,” sums up the founder, who wants to push the limits
Chris, qui est âgé de 16 ans, s’est join: Chris, who is 16, joined Philo-Boxe just before Cobra, after playing ping-pong for a long time. With the forced break imposed by the pandemic, he missed training. “When I come here, I’m more comfortable than in class. It’s really welcoming,” he says. Like his teammate, he appreciates the time set aside for philosophical discussions. “It lets us learn things we don’t learn at school,” says Chris, who plans to study programming at CEGEP next year.
Chris, prêt à boxer et à discuter.Photo:: Chris, ready to box and to talk. Photo: Pablo Ortiz
Chris témoigne de l’énorme pression qu’é: Chris speaks to the enormous pressure young people feel, particularly those who struggle at school. Among his friends in the neighbourhood, many have dropped out to go to work. Although he does well at school, Chris doesn’t find happiness there. “I don’t like the school system. Nobody likes school. You don’t learn how to act in life there. They don’t explain what’s happening, why, how we could do things,” he believes. He also alludes to the generational conflict that pits young people against those who came before them. “Parents think we should live the same thing they did, but it’s not the same,” he says. “They tend to have a lot of prejudices and have a hard time accepting things from our generation, listening to what we say – they put a lot of pressure on us.” Before heading back to the training mat, Chris urges his peers to stick with what they love. “No matter what we choose, we really have to go all in. It’ll make us love life.”
Philo-Boxe, qui est un organisme sans bu: Philo-Boxe, a non-profit organization (NPO), relies on its own means to fund its operations. It has not received any government grants since its beginnings. “We can’t wait for the government to give us money, our job is to act. We’re here to support the community,” he says. This week, Public Security Minister Geneviève Guilbault announced that $52 million would be distributed as part of a crime prevention plan. Nearly $11.3 million would thus be allocated over five years to a program for preventing delinquency through sports, arts and culture, in which Philo-Boxe’s mission would fit perfectly. “It’s good, it will help community organizations create new programs,” believes Mr. Coppry.
Cependant, la façon dont les subventions: However, the way government grants are allocated is a problem, in his view. “It has to be for a specific project,” he explains. Minister Guilbault indicated the government’s desire to change its practice with the Programme de financement de la mission des organismes communautaires de travail de rue en prévention de la criminalité. The initiative provides $20.2 million over four years starting in 2022, which will directly benefit the organizations’ missions. While the money is welcome, for Karim Coppry, it isn’t everything. “There’s some soul-searching to be done,” says the coach, who hopes that people in positions of power will become aware of that.
Le travail qu’accomplit Karim Coppry ave: The work Karim Coppry does with Philo-Boxe is absolutely necessary in the eyes of the family of Jannai Dopwell-Bailey, the 16-year-old who was murdered in front of his Côte-des-Neiges school on October 18 by other young people. At the vigil held in his honour, several loved ones called for more services for young people in the neighbourhood. “I think we need more programs, especially for children of colour. We need basketball, leadership, robotics, swimming, music programs – we need opportunities and access to give teenagers things to do so they’re not out on the street,” said Tyrese Dopwell-Bailey, the victim’s brother, on that occasion. “I want a place where young people and the community can play basketball, play music, meet each other. There is nothing here for young people. They’re in the street,” his mother lamented.
« J’espère que les élus de Côte-des-Neig: “I hope the elected officials of Côte-des-Neiges are working on putting programs in place for young people so that we no longer have to witness this kind of thing,” added Onica John, the cousin of the young man who was killed. Here’s hoping their wishes are granted in the near future. <l1>philoboxe.ca</l1>
